facts.claim: "Bruddanem" is track 8 on JID's album The Forever Story, released August 26, 2022 on Dreamville/Interscope, and runs 3:55.
The song was produced by DJ Khalil, TU!, Christo and Yuli.
Credits list DJ Khalil, Neal Pogue, Yuli and Christo as producers, with Yuli as additional producer. Mustafa the Poet is credited for spoken word.
Engineering credits: John Kadadu recorded it, Derek Ali and Curtis "Sircut" Bye mixed it, and Nicolas De Porcel mastered it.
Songwriting credits include JID (Destin Route), Lil Durk (Durk Banks), DJ Khalil, Neal Pogue and Daniel Seeff.
The Forever Story was executive produced by Christo, who had 10 credits across its 16 tracks.
The title plays on the Chicago slang word "foenem", meaning family. JID and Lil Durk pledge loyalty to their brothers, both blood and not.
A double music video for "Bruddanem" and "Crack Sandwich" was released in October 2022. Mac Grant and Chad Tennies directed it.
One review praises JID's sung chorus over an old-school instrumental. It also says Durk's verse covers rivals and brothers who would slide for him.
The Forever Story is a conceptual sequel to JID's 2017 debut The Never Story. It was recorded from 2020 to 2022 and focuses on JID's upbringing and family.
JID is an Atlanta rapper born Destin Route. He signed to J. Cole's Dreamville in 2017 and first appeared with the 2015 EP DiCaprio.

research.lineage: The song belongs to Atlanta lyrical, soul-inflected hip-hop on Dreamville, and it pairs JID with Chicago drill-era rapper Lil Durk on a loyalty-to-family theme.

draft:
The last thing **Bruddanem** asks of anyone is gentle: "Take care of your skin, take care of your liver." It arrives after nearly four minutes of Glocks, blocks spun, and opps hit, and it changes what the rest of the song meant. All that menace was a way of saying I love you in the only words that felt safe to use.

The title bends Chicago's "foenem," slang for family, into something JID can carry home to Atlanta. Pairing him with Lil Durk makes sense of it. JID's corner is lyrical, soul-leaning Dreamville rap, and Durk comes from the drill era. They meet on one subject, loyalty to brothers by blood and by choice. JID sings the chorus, and the hook works by stacking: the same title phrase lands at the end of every line until the repetition sounds like a vow. Layered, harmonized backing voices answer the lead in a call-and-response. Under them sit a sustained low synth bass and a soft pad. A small, repeating synth figure runs high over the top, and a tight snare and quick hi-hats keep the groove steady at a moderate tempo. It's clean and dry, with room left for the words.

Those words are where the feeling lives. The long middle verse goes back to childhood. Summers when "somebody dead and somebody scared, so nobody saw," a grown-up laid off and stuck in bed, bail money, kids to feed. Then a quiet confession: "Got a whippin' for nothin', that's somethin' my brother did." The narrator took the punishment and kept quiet, and he tells it with pride, not resentment. That's where the loyalty comes from. It was taught through silence, sore skin, and knowing the brother would have done the same.

Pride and grief sit side by side here without settling. One line boasts and mourns at the same time: "My brother gon' slide, but two of my brothers had died." Another remembers the power knocked out and sleeping by the window, hungry. The bravado is real, but so is the hole under it. When the closing lines turn to "I see you, I love you," with two straps at dinner and a promise not to let anyone wither, the song stops pretending those are different feelings. Mustafa the Poet is credited for spoken word, and the producers include DJ Khalil, Christo and Yuli. One reviewer called the beat old-school, and the hook does have that warm, settled pull.

It sticks because it lets you hear protectiveness the way these brothers learned it: half threat, half caretaking, and impossible to pull apart.
